section_summary: The section finishes a report on Japanese prices, wages, government finances and bank lending, then turns to 1948 correspondence about economic deconcentration, recovery, aid, reparations and export policy. It includes press clippings, a Soviet statement on Japanese industry, a conversation about Chinese opposition to aid for Japan, and a request for economic research materials. The final Army letter continues beyond page 359.

subfiles.title: Economic Conditions in Japan, concluding pages
subfiles.from: Economic and Scientific Section, General Headquarters
subfiles.about: Analyzes mid-1948 Japanese prices, wages, fiscal policy, debt and bank credit.
subfiles.summary: The report attributes rising consumer prices chiefly to black-market staple foods and assesses the effects of new official prices and wage pressure. It reviews 1947–48 tax collections and the larger 1948–49 budget, then forecasts renewed government borrowing and currency expansion. Tables show national debt holdings and bank loans to business.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement form for Tokyo despatch 564
subfiles.about: Designates a copy of Tokyo despatch 564 as the record copy.
subfiles.summary: A replacement copy is marked for return to Central Records.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Economic Conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a June 1948 economic conditions report and highlights production and price developments.
subfiles.summary: The cover despatch forwards the report and notes improved coal output, weak textiles and sharply rising prices.

subfiles.title: Progress of Economic Deconcentration Program
subfiles.from: Office of the Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports company designations, reorganization procedures and disputes over Nippon Soda.
subfiles.summary: The despatch says many initially designated companies had been released and only a fraction were expected to undergo structural reorganization. It describes review procedures and tension between the Anti-Trust and Cartels Division and the Deconcentration Review Board over Nippon Soda.

subfiles.title: Japanese Reds Fight SCAP's Fiscal Policy
subfiles.about: Reports Welsh's claim that Japanese Communists opposed business deconcentration.
subfiles.summary: Four copies of the same article quote Edward Welsh defending deconcentration as a way to create independent, competing firms. He alleges Communist disruption and responds to criticism by Raymond Moley.

subfiles.title: Plans for Reorganization of Key Industries Pushed
subfiles.about: Lists pending reorganization plans in textiles, steel, chemicals and motion pictures.
subfiles.summary: Welsh describes designations and planned reorganizations across four Japanese industries.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo despatch 596
subfiles.about: Summarizes despatch 596 and the dispute over Nippon Soda's reorganization.
subfiles.summary: Notes fewer designated firms and friction between Welsh and the Review Board.

subfiles.title: Restoration of Japan to Self-Support
subfiles.about: Proposes linking United States aid to Japanese economic performance and paying occupation costs currently.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman proposes Japanese responsibility for an approved recovery plan, regular SCAP performance reports and aid decisions tied to results. He also urges payment to Japan for occupation costs beginning in fiscal 1950.

subfiles.title: Reparations levels and primary war facilities
subfiles.about: Explains revised proposed Japanese industrial retention levels and treatment of war facilities.
subfiles.summary: The writer defends a five-million-ton steel capacity and proposes 500,000 metric tons of steel shipbuilding capacity in initial talks. The letter permits limited SCAP retention of primary war facilities needed for occupation and seeks schedules ensuring allocated reparations are removed.

subfiles.title: Japanese Reparations
subfiles.about: Sets out proposed United States policy for Japanese reparations and allocation.
subfiles.summary: The proposal would end most advance transfers, define industrial equipment available for claims, and allow SCAP to retain specified equipment needed for occupation. It calls for claims, allocations and removal schedules through the Far Eastern Commission, while contemplating unilateral action if agreement fails.

subfiles.title: Japanese export pricing and Young Mission recommendations
subfiles.about: Questions a reported Japanese export pricing system and seeks Army action on exchange policy.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman asks whether a press report about a multiple-rate export system is accurate. He argues that continued delay in implementing National Advisory Council policy and the Young Mission recommendations is unwarranted.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposed reply to the Philippines
subfiles.about: Suggests wording for a reply concerning Philippine reparations from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fearey considers acknowledging the value of facilities already received by the Philippines.

subfiles.title: Statement on Soviet proposals for Japanese industry
subfiles.to: United States member, Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Provides a discretionary response and questions about Soviet proposals for Japanese industry.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum welcomes peaceful Japanese production and trade while suggesting questions about Soviet definitions of war industry and proposed controls. It advises against taking the lead in debate.

subfiles.title: Draft statement on Soviet proposals for Japanese industry
subfiles.about: Drafts questions about peaceful industry, war industry and postwar controls.
subfiles.summary: An annotated draft asks how the Soviet proposals would define and control Japanese war industry.

subfiles.title: Statement of the Soviet Delegation on Level of Economic Life in Japan
subfiles.about: Advocates unrestricted peaceful Japanese industry alongside a prohibition on war industry.
subfiles.summary: The statement argues that peaceful industrial growth would improve Japanese living standards, exports and regional trade. It proposes banning Japanese war industry and establishing multiyear controls by powers concerned with preventing renewed aggression.

subfiles.title: Despatch 124 forwarding conversation with Professor Chang Hsi-je
subfiles.from: John M. Cabot, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.to: J. Leighton Stuart, American Ambassador, Nanking
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum on Chinese views of United States aid to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Cabot transmits his conversation with Professor Chang Hsi-je.

subfiles.title: Conversation between Professor Chang Hsi-je and John M. Cabot
subfiles.about: Records a discussion of United States aid to Japan, the Chinese civil war and Chinese Communist prospects.
subfiles.summary: Chang describes Chinese fears of Japan's recovery but says opposition to American support for the Kuomintang is the deeper issue. Cabot explains United States concern about Communist expansion. They discuss whether Chinese Communists would later seek American trade and capital.

subfiles.title: Request for information on Japan's economy
subfiles.about: Requests reports and sources on Japanese trade, industry, finance and zaibatsu liquidation.
subfiles.summary: Kanzaki seeks material for a master's thesis on Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Albert T. Kanzaki
subfiles.from: R. Burr Smith, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Supplies publications and directs Kanzaki to other agencies for Japanese economic information.
subfiles.summary: The reply encloses two publications and suggests Army and Tariff Commission sources.

subfiles.title: Army reply on restoration of Japan to self-support
subfiles.from: Office of the Under Secretary of the Army
subfiles.about: Responds to Saltzman's proposals on occupation costs and Japanese responsibility for recovery.
subfiles.summary: The Army agrees that Japanese self-support is a major objective but rejects the proposed pay-as-you-go occupation-cost arrangement, citing budget, legal and congressional concerns. Its discussion of transferring recovery responsibility to the Japanese government continues beyond this section.
